en.title: Brian Jacques' Redwall: An Epic Tale of Woodland Heroes
en.summary: Discover the enduring charm of Brian Jacques' Redwall series, a literary phenomenon that continues to captivate readers with its grand adventures and beloved characters. From humble beginnings, this saga of talking animals has spawned a multimedia empire.
en.body:
When you think of talking animal epics, **Brian Jacques’ Redwall** stands in a category all its own. What began as a passion project, penned by hand by Jacques for children at a school for the blind, blossomed into a publishing phenomenon. The initial manuscript, a formidable 800 pages, caught the eye of a publisher who saw its immense potential, offering Jacques a five-book contract despite its unusual length for the early 1980s. This gamble paid off spectacularly, leading to 22 novels released between 1986 and 2011, alongside an animated television series, video games, merchandise, and more.

The world of Redwall is a vibrant tapestry woven with the lives of its woodland inhabitants. At its heart is the peaceful Redwall Abbey, nestled beside the Mossflower Forest. This sanctuary is primarily home to mice, but also shelters squirrels, moles, hedgehogs, voles, shrews, and is defended by formidable figures like an indomitable badger and an intrepid hare. Their peaceful existence is, however, threatened by a host of menacing predators: rats, ferrets, stoats, foxes, and the chillingly named snake, Asmodeus. The very first novel, **Redwall**, sets the stage with an epic plot, drawing inspiration from classical literature and adventure fiction.

## A World of Woodland Warriors

The narrative of **Redwall** often centers on a young hero thrust into extraordinary circumstances. In the inaugural novel, the story follows Matthias, a novice mouse at Redwall Abbey, who becomes the chosen hero. Jacques meticulously crafted a world where these creatures, despite their small stature, undertake grand quests and face down formidable evils. His ability to imbue these animal characters with distinct personalities and motivations is a key reason for the series' lasting appeal. The detailed descriptions of feasts, the abbey's architecture, and the surrounding forests create an immersive experience that has drawn generations of readers into its embrace.

## The Enduring Legacy of Redwall

For legions of fans, the **Redwall** series represents more than just children's fantasy; it's a beloved world filled with courage, friendship, and the triumph of good over evil. The news of a planned Netflix film adaptation, though recently canceled, underscores the enduring cultural impact of Jacques' creation. Even with the series concluding its novel run in 2011, its continued presence in print and the streaming availability of the animated show demonstrate its lasting power. Readers fondly recall the intricate plots, the heartwarming camaraderie among the abbey dwellers, and the thrilling battles against their foes, proving that the tales spun in Redwall Abbey resonate deeply across generations.

## What's Next

While the Netflix film adaptation has been canceled, details regarding any new adaptations or continuations of the **Redwall** universe have not yet been announced. Fans can, however, revisit the original novels and the animated series to relive the magic of Redwall Abbey.

By Judith Tarr | Published on August 3, 2026 Comment 0 Share New Share Redwall &url= target=”_blank” title=”Twitter”> Redwall ” target=”_blank” title=”Pinterest”> Brian Jacques’ Redwall was a publishing phenomenon from the very beginning. Jacques wrote it (by hand, 800 pages’ worth) for children at a school for the blind in Liverpool, showed it to a writer friend who passed it on to his own publisher, and even though the book was nearly twice as long as the usual chapter book in the early 1980s, the publisher offered him a five-book contract. The gamble paid off richly: 22 novels between 1986 and 2011, an animated television series, games, merch, picture books, cookbooks, all the trappings of a runaway success. It’s still in print and the series (originally aired from 1999 to 2002) is still streaming, though the heavily promoted Netflix film has, alas, been canceled . It all begins with the story of a mouse named Matthias, a brand-new novice in Redwall Abbey near the Mossflower Forest. There are no humans in this world. The peaceful brothers and sisters of Redwall are primarily mice, but they share the abbey and the forest with numerous woodland creatures: squirrels, moles, hedgehogs, voles, shrews, an indomitable badger, an intrepid hare, and various other animals and birds. They have enemies, too: rats, ferrets, stoats, foxes, and a terrifying snake named Asmodeus (“Asmodeussssssss….”). The first volume is epic in plot as well as length. Jacques was well read in classical literature as well as adventure fiction and children’s stories. Matthias is the chosen hero, the fated victor, avatar of the legendary Martin the Warrior, complete with quest to find Martin’s tomb and win his armor, shield, and sword. His fated enemy is the terrible Cluny the Scourge, the one-eyed rat who wields his tail like a bullwhip and tips it with a poisoned dart. Matthias and his friends are flawed and, dare I say it, human. They squabble, bicker, make mistakes. Sometimes they do bad things, either because they’re compelled or because they have good but misguided intentions. They grow and learn and change, and when they come into conflict with each other, they eventually shake paws and make up. Cluny and his mob of cutthroats have no redeeming features. Even when they pretend to be good, they’re plotting evil, sniggering at the well-intentioned fools who buy what they’re selling. There’s no kindness in them, no goodwill and no gratitude. They’re bad to the bone. In between the two are the aggressive and warlike sparrows. At the beginning they own the upper reaches of the abbey, beating off anyone who tries to invade their domain.
